name: find files by name
description: recursively list files matching a glob under <dir>
gotchas: quote the glob ('*.log') so the shell doesn't expand it before find sees it
explanation: -type f restricts to regular files; drop it to match dirs/symlinks too. Use -iname for case-insensitive.

name: find and delete files
description: delete every entry matching the glob under <dir>
gotchas: -delete is destructive and has no confirmation — run the find without it first to preview
-delete must come AFTER the tests; find evaluates left-to-right

name: chmod only directories
description: apply a mode to directories only, recursively
explanation: '{} +' batches many paths into one chmod call (fast); '{} \;' runs one chmod per file (slow but needed when the command can take only one arg).
portability: -exec ... + is POSIX and on GNU+BSD alike.

name: biggest items in a dir
description: size of each child of <dir>, sorted smallest→largest
gotchas: the glob skips dotfiles; use du -sh <dir>/* <dir>/.[!.]* or 'du -sh <dir>/.[!.]* ' to include them
portability: sort -h (human numeric) is GNU coreutils; BSD sort lacks it.

name: disk free per filesystem
description: show mounted filesystems with human-readable sizes

examples.note: -i shows inode usage instead of blocks

name: list block devices + filesystems
description: tree of disks/partitions with FS type, label, UUID and mountpoint

name: chmod symbolic
description: add/remove/set permission bits without computing octal
explanation: u=user/owner, g=group, o=other, a=all; + adds, - removes, = sets exactly.

name: recursive chown
description: change owner and group of a tree

examples.note: reclaim ownership of a dir you copied as root

gotchas: -R follows into the whole tree; double-check <path> before running as root

name: create a symlink
description: make <linkname> point at <target>

examples.note: -f replace, -n don't deref an existing link-to-dir

gotchas: a relative <target> is resolved relative to the link's location, not your cwd — prefer absolute targets or cd there first

name: create gzip tarball
description: bundle paths into a compressed archive
explanation: Mnemonic: 'create zee file' / 'extract zee file' / 'taste zee file'. Use J for .tar.xz, j for .tar.bz2.

name: find a process
description: list processes whose command line matches <name>

examples.note: the [s] trick hides the grep itself from results

gotchas: plain grep also matches its own line; use pgrep <name> for a clean PID list

name: kill processes by command line
description: send a signal to every process whose full command line matches

examples.note: -f matches the whole command, not just the binary name
SIGKILL if it won't die on the default SIGTERM

gotchas: -f can match more than you expect (including the shell that launched it) — preview with pgrep -af <pattern> first

name: listening TCP sockets
description: show listening TCP ports with the owning process

examples.note: need root to see PIDs of other users' sockets

explanation: t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, n=numeric (don't resolve names), p=process. ss replaces the deprecated netstat.

name: interface addresses (brief)
description: one line per interface: name, state, addresses

examples.note: quick 'what's my IP / which NICs are up'

name: show routing table
description: kernel IPv4 routes incl. the default gateway

examples.note: show which route/interface a destination would use

name: follow a service's logs
description: tail systemd journal for one unit, live
explanation: -u filters by unit, -f follows, -b limits to a boot, -p sets max priority (err, warning, info...).

name: service state + recent logs
description: show whether a unit is active/enabled and its last log lines

examples.note: enable at boot AND start right now

gotchas: enable ≠ start: 'enable' only sets boot behaviour; add --now (or 'start') to also run it immediately

name: in-place find/replace
description: edit a file in place, replacing every match on each line

examples.note: g = all matches per line, not just the first

gotchas: GNU sed: -i takes an optional suffix attached (-i.bak). BSD/macOS sed REQUIRES an argument: -i '' for no backup.
portability: GNU vs BSD sed differ on -i — the #1 cross-platform sed gotcha.

name: print a column
description: print the Nth whitespace-separated field of each line

examples.note: -F: split on colon instead of whitespace

explanation: $0 is the whole line, $1..$NF the fields, NF = field count. Default separator is runs of whitespace.

name: count and rank duplicates
description: tally identical lines and order by frequency, most common first

examples.cmd: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

gotchas: uniq only collapses ADJACENT duplicates — you must sort first or counts are wrong

name: run detached from the terminal
description: start a long job that survives logout, with output redirected

examples.note: keeps running after you close the shell

explanation: nohup ignores SIGHUP (sent on terminal close); & backgrounds it; 2>&1 folds stderr into the same log. Consider 'disown' or a systemd unit / tmux for anything important.

name: re-run a command on a timer
description: repeat a command every N seconds and show the latest output full-screen

examples.note: -d highlights what changed since last tick

gotchas: quote the command (and any pipes) or watch only re-runs the first part

name: download a file robustly
description: fetch a URL to a file, failing loudly and following redirects

examples.note: the (risky) pipe-to-shell pattern — read the script first

explanation: -f fail on HTTP errors (no 404 HTML saved), -s silent, -S still show errors, -L follow redirects.

name: memory usage
description: RAM and swap totals/used/free in human units

examples.note: the 'available' column is the realistic 'how much can I still use'

gotchas: 'free' looks low and 'used' high because Linux caches files in RAM — judge by the 'available' column, not 'free'
